s: Part three.
Path-specific rules.

By the end of this part, you'll know how to make a convention load only for certain files, how the patterns work, how to debug a rule that isn't loading, and when to pick a rule over a subfolder CLAUDE.md.
Plain version.
The whiteboard by the door is read to everybody who walks in.
A sign taped to the door of one room is read only by the people who go into that room.
A convention that governs the payments code should cost nothing on a day when nobody opens the payments code.
And there's a catch worth saying up front.
A sign works only when someone opens that particular door.
And it cannot stop anyone doing anything.
The technical name is a path-scoped rule.
You put a markdown file in the .claude/rules/ folder.
At the top, you give it frontmatter with a field called paths.
That field holds a list of file patterns, called globs.
The rule loads only when Claude works with a file matching one of those patterns.
What about a rule in that folder with no paths field?
It loads unconditionally at launch.
Every session.
And rules in that folder are found by their own mechanism.
You don't import them.
The course presenter flagged this as the exam answer for conditional file-type rules.
And he repeated it on purpose, so it would stick.
Hold on to this line.
The rules folder plus paths frontmatter is the answer for conditional, file-type conventions.
His sample question was different rules for TypeScript files and Terraform files.
The answer: rule files with path patterns.
One for the TypeScript source.
One for the Terraform folder.
Question one.
Practice question D3-010.
Here's the scenario.
A monorepo with fourteen packages.
Test files ending in .test.ts and .spec.ts are scattered through all of them, often beside the source files.
The team wants strict test conventions, like never use the any type, and always declare return types in test helpers.
Those conventions should load only when Claude works on a test file.
Never during ordinary source edits.
And no team owns test conventions per package.
What's the setup?
Take a second.
The answer.
A single rule file, .claude/rules/testing.md, with paths set to `**/*.test.ts` and `**/*.spec.ts`.
Those patterns match test files at any depth.
Plain version.
It's like a recipe card marked desserts only, that comes out whenever someone bakes, whichever kitchen they're in.
Taping a copy inside every kitchen door means people read it while making soup too.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a CLAUDE.md in each of the fourteen packages.
Why?
Directory files scope by location, not by file type.
So they also load during source edits in those packages.
And the text is duplicated fourteen times.
Wrong: a section in the root CLAUDE.md, headed for files matching test patterns.
Why?
CLAUDE.md has no conditional scoping.
That heading is just text.
Wrong: an import of a testing document from the root.
Why?
Imports expand at launch.
So the conventions load in every session.
The deciding words are file type, scattered, and only when.
So remember.
When the condition is a file type rather than a folder, reach for a rule with paths.
Now glob syntax.
The exam builds troubleshooting questions on it.
Plain version.
A sign reading rules for the ground floor is not read by anyone working upstairs, even though it's the same building.
If you meant every floor, the sign has to say all floors.
In exam terms.
A single asterisk matches anything within one directory level.
A double asterisk matches any number of directories.
So. `**/*.ts` matches TypeScript anywhere. `src/**/*` matches everything under the source folder. `*.md` on its own matches only markdown files at the project root.
And braces let you list several extensions at once, as in `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`.
Question two.
Practice question D3-011.
Here's the scenario.
A repository keeps invoice schemas under a schemas folder, organized into subfolders like schemas/invoices/v2.
A rule has paths set to `schemas/*.json`.
While Claude edits a file three levels down, /memory doesn't list the rule, and Claude ignores its conventions.
What's the root cause?
Take a second.
The answer.
The single asterisk stops at the first level.
So the pattern covers only files sitting directly in schemas.
The fix is `schemas/**/*.json`.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: path rules load only in sessions started from the folder containing the matched files.
Why?
They don't.
Rules live centrally, and fire on matching reads wherever you started.
Wrong: rules are discovered only when the root CLAUDE.md imports them.
Why?
They aren't.
And an import would load the content unconditionally anyway.
Wrong: the pattern's brace expansions exceed the budget.
Why?
There are no braces in this pattern.
That last distractor is built on a real edge case.
So know it.
Brace groups multiply.
And a rule's whole paths list shares a budget of one thousand expanded patterns.
A pattern that would exceed the budget is used unexpanded.
So its literal braces match nothing.
Similarly, a square bracket that cannot be read as a valid bracket expression makes that one pattern match nothing.
The rule's other patterns keep working.
Both fail quietly.
That's why they make good troubleshooting distractors.
But you only reach for them when the pattern actually contains braces or brackets.
Hold on to this line.
One star is one folder level.
Two stars is any depth.
Question three.
Practice question D3-012.
This is the mirror problem.
Here's the scenario.
A developer added a Terraform rule, Terraform being a tool for describing cloud infrastructure as code.
The rule has naming and module conventions, and no frontmatter.
Now frontend engineers see Claude suggesting Terraform-style snake case names in React components.
And every session carries the Terraform text, even when no infrastructure file is touched.
All Terraform files live under an infra folder.
What's going on, and what's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
A rule with no paths loads every session.
That single fact explains both symptoms.
The context cost, and the cross-contamination.
The fix is to add frontmatter with paths set to `infra/**/*.tf`.
Plain version.
A notice meant for the garage mechanics is pinned in the main entrance.
So the receptionist starts using mechanic jargon on the phone.
Moving the notice to the garage door fixes it.
Writing mechanics only on it, while leaving it in the entrance, doesn't.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: move it to the personal rules folder, so the frontend team stops getting it.
Why?
That removes it from the infrastructure team, and from the pipeline too.
Wrong: add a first line saying apply these only to Terraform files.
Why?
A prose scope statement still loads every session, and relies on judgment.
Wrong: move it into the root CLAUDE.md, under a Terraform-only heading.
Why?
Headings don't scope anything.
So remember.
A rule without paths is always on.
Add paths to make it conditional.
Now debugging.
The course presenter flagged this as an exam scenario as well.
How do you check whether Claude is loading your files?
The answer he gave is the /memory command.
If a file you expected isn't in its list, that's your problem to fix.
Perhaps a naming or configuration mistake.
A small source disagreement here.
It's worth a moment.
The transcript says /memory lists what loaded.
The command reference says it opens memory files so you can edit them.
It does both.
In the video's demonstration, it shows project and user memory, and which files are in play.
And you can open them from there.
For the exam, the scenario is using /memory to see what loaded.
Question four.
Practice question D3-013.
Here's the scenario.
A developer added a refund-tool rule, with paths set to `tools/refund/**/*.py`.
They report Claude still ignores the refund conventions while editing tools/refund/policy.py.
They want to fix it.
What should they do first?
Take a second.
The answer.
Run /memory after Claude has read that file, and check whether the rule is listed.
Plain version.
When a guest says they never got your note, first check whether it's actually on the noticeboard.
Don't repaint it in red, or glue copies to every wall, until you know which problem you're fixing.
In exam terms, the timing matters.
Path-scoped rules load when Claude reads a matching file.
So check after the read.
If the rule is absent, the problem is configuration.
Like the glob, or the location.
If it's present, the problem lies elsewhere.
Now the wrong turns.
They're all remedies before diagnosis.
Wrong: copy the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md.
Why?
It's a global fix that adds permanent cost to every session.
And it may not address the cause.
Wrong: rewrite with mandatory headings.
Why?
Emphasis cannot help a rule that never loaded.
Wrong: convert it into a user-only skill.
Why?
It changes the mechanism before knowing what failed.
And it makes correct behavior depend on someone remembering to invoke it.
The constraint word is first.
When a stem asks what to do first, the answer is almost always to diagnose.
Two related tools from the notes.
First.
The /context command lists which memory files actually loaded.
Second.
A hook event called InstructionsLoaded can log which instruction files loaded, and when.
That's the right tool for debugging rules that load lazily.
Now the compaction trap.
It connects to the chapter on context management.
Here's the scenario.
A path-scoped rule for database migrations works reliably early in a long session.
Then the session compacts, meaning the conversation is summarized to free space.
After that, Claude proposes a destructive column drop, while still working in the migrations folder.
Why?
The root project CLAUDE.md is re-read and re-injected after compaction.
But subfolder CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules are not.
A path rule reloads only the next time Claude reads a matching file.
If Claude keeps editing without a fresh read, the rule is simply no longer in the window.
Distractors will offer three wrong causes.
That rules become inert by design after compaction.
That compaction rewrote the file on disk.
Or that double asterisk became invalid.
None of those is true.
And if the convention must survive regardless of context state?
Two options.
Promote it to a PreToolUse hook that inspects the edit.
Or move it into the root file, and accept the always-on cost.
Also note.
Path rules trigger on reading a matching file.
Not on every tool call.
Now the contrast segment the exam loves.
Path-scoped rule versus subfolder CLAUDE.md.
Both load conditionally.
The deciding question is usually ownership, and shape.
A subfolder CLAUDE.md sits with its code.
It loads when Claude works in that folder.
That suits a monorepo where each package owner maintains a file beside the code they own.
That was D3-004.
A central rule in the rules folder fires on a glob.
That suits a file type, or a convention spanning scattered paths.
And it keeps all conventions reviewable in one directory.
That was D3-010.
A subfolder CLAUDE.md cannot target file patterns at all.
A self-check from the notes puts it well.
Say you have three services with incompatible testing conventions.
Both answers are defensible.
Choose per-directory files when each service team should own its file.
Choose central rules when you want everything reviewable in one place.
What you must never do is leave all three in the root file.
Every session pays for two irrelevant sets.
And their contradictions degrade adherence to all three.
And neither mechanism is a gate.
A rule that must hold every time belongs in a hook.
One last detail, about priority.
Personal rules in ~/.claude/rules/ load before project rules.
The documentation describes this as giving project rules higher priority.
It's a load-order fact.
So don't confuse it with the skill collision order from part two.
That's part three.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Rules with paths load only on matching reads.
They're not re-injected after compaction.
And you debug them with /memory.
